pitch_detail.notes: Where the climbers' path meets the cliff band, look for a rappel anchor slung over a tangle of dead tree roots: scramble the short class 3 gully beside it, then follow a dirt path up through heather to a grassy, rocky knoll. Drop about 50 ft off the far side and cross talus or snow to the base of the chimneys. A short 4th-class rock step here can sit above weak snow bridges early in the season.

The chimneys are broad gullies rather than true chimneys: roughly 1,000–1,200 vertical ft of 2nd–3rd class dirt path broken by exposed 4th-class steps, ascending leftward. The right gully shows rock scoured clean by boot traffic; mossy or lichen-covered rock means you are off route. The hardest moves are low in the lower chimneys. Slung anchors sit atop most 4th-class steps; helmets matter under other parties.

Walk briefly across the top of the White Salmon Glacier to a rock outcrop with bivy platforms and meltwater pools, then climb Winnie's Slide, a steep snow slope of roughly 150–200 ft (angles quoted range from about 45° to near 60° at the top). Go straight up its right side, then traverse left to a narrow rock rib. Crampons are effectively mandatory; late in summer it melts to glacial ice needing screws and a second tool.

Climb the left side of the Upper Curtis Glacier, turn right above its crevasses, and traverse the gentle rolling slopes beneath the cliffs on your left, climbing then losing a little height to reach the base of Hell's Highway. In early summer the glacier is usually fully snow-covered; by late season expect exposed crevasses and sagging snow bridges that make this the most serious glacier ground on the route.

Hell's Highway is a steep step of snow or alpine ice leading up onto the Sulphide Glacier; it looks intimidating from below but is short. Two lines are used: the right side is shorter and more exposed (a shortcut beside a hogsback-like feature), the left longer and less exposed. Expect front-pointing when firm; carry pickets or screws, and watch for cavernous crevasses under sagging bridges around its base.

pitch_detail.pitch: Sulphide Glacier to the summit pyramid
pitch_detail.notes: At the top of Hell's Highway turn sharply left and parallel the ridge, joining the Sulphide Glacier route for the gentle glacier walk up to the base of the summit pyramid. Parties commonly stash crampons and axes at the rock. Rope up on the glacier: it is broad and moderate but still carries crevasses, and the return in the afternoon is on softer snow.

The standard finish climbs the central gully of the summit pyramid, about 600 vertical ft of exposed class 3–4 through a network of gullies with much loose rock; rockfall from parties above is the main hazard, so avoid stacking up below others. The gully is descended by downclimbing plus two or three rappels from slung horns and fixed rings. A cleaner, harder southeast rib (roughly 5.4–5.6) is the alternative.

review.changed: Same six labelled sections, each rewritten with location, terrain, route-finding and hazard detail; Section 5 given its sourced 60 m length. Added one new stage (Sulphide Glacier to the summit pyramid) that the stored table skipped between Hell's Highway and the pyramid. 6 → 7 entries.
sources_consulted: https://www.cmc.org/education-adventure/trips/routes-places/mount-shuksan (search summary: pyramid central gully exposed class 4, 600 ft)
review.other_findings: pitches=3 does not describe this route (it is a multi-section glacier route, not three pitches). The Section 5 stored note called Hell's Highway a 'second steep step up to the Sulphide Glacier' — correct; one source misdescribes it as ~300 ft, the majority give ~60 m.

pitch_detail.notes: Leave the Boston Glacier across the moat or bergschrund at the face's margin, which widens through the season, and climb the rock just below and to the left of the large ice patch on the lower face. The section is rated old-style grade III and was first protected with a few pitons; expect no fixed gear, and treat this outline with caution because the face sees very few ascents.

The technical centre of the route: a sustained ice patch at about 50°. It faces north and has thinned across the range since the first ascent, so check that it still holds enough ice for screws before committing. Everything on the upper face drains through this patch, making it the place most exposed to falling rock and ice from above.

Above the ice the face stays steep, but the rock is stacked in upward-dipping slabs that give holds and make it easier than it appears from below; it leads directly to the summit. Do not plan to reverse the face: the descent is by another route, and Forbidden has no easy way off by any line.

review.changed: Same three labelled sections; notes expanded (bergschrund start, ice thinning, rockfall funnel, upslab character) and the section lengths from the only first-hand account (300 / 300 / 600 ft) added as lengthM. Grade chips tightened.
review.other_findings: Only one source exists (the 1961 first-ascent note); no modern trip report was found. The stored overview calls this 'a steep snow-and-ice face ... sustained steep ice climbing', but the FA describes a mostly rock route (300 ft rock, 300 ft ice, 600 ft upslab rock) — the overview overstates the ice. Stored `rappels` says 'Same as East Ledges: ~5 single-rope rappels' while descent_text says descend the West Ridge; the FA says only 'normal route'. These two fields disagree.

pitch_detail.notes: From the top of the snow and ice approach, solo or simul-climb steep, somewhat loose 4th to low-5th class rock up the rib toward the summit. The rock here is the worst on the route: move carefully and keep the party close to limit rockfall. Rope up for real where the rib narrows into a knife-edge.

Cross the exposed knife-edge section of the rib, staying on the crest. The climbing is moderate but the position is airy on both sides; protect it as a proper pitch even if the lower ground was simul-climbed.

The rib steepens into the crux: stay true to the crest, stemming and crack climbing on solid granite flakes. Some parties find the ground just before the crest somewhat dirty and sparsely protected. The crux grade is 5.8 in rock shoes; it is often described as about 5.6 in the boots most parties wear for the approach.

Where the rib blends into the face, head up and left into a wide chimney where the rock steepens; old fixed gear marks it. The rock is poor near the chimney's base, then improves markedly as it opens onto the true northwest face, with excellent crack systems above.

Continue up low-5th to 5.6 cracks and flakes on good rock to the summit, joining the upper West Ridge just below the top. Much of this upper ground is commonly simul-climbed; parties who do so should keep enough gear in to protect a fall on juggy but exposed terrain.

review.changed: Same five labels kept; notes rewritten from four trip reports and the route page (rock quality, where to rope up, chimney position and fixed gear, boot vs shoe grading, joining the West Ridge). Pitch 1-2 given its sourced ~500 ft length; '4th-low 5th' and 'low 5th-5.6' grade strings replaced by single grade tokens.
review.other_findings: Commitment grade is given as III (route page) and IV (spokalpine, guide service); stored grade says III. Pitch counts vary widely by source (7 pitches / 1,200 ft on the route page; four 60 m pitches plus ~800 ft simul in one report; '8 to 11 more pitches' in a guide description) — the stored pitches=7 is one of several defensible values.

pitch_detail.notes: From a horn near the summit, rappel straight down the northeast side of the summit block. These are the first three of about five single-rope rappels (roughly 400 ft in all) that lead onto the ledge system. Inspect every anchor: the stations are slung tat on rock, not bolts.

A short, grassy traverse east across exposed ground brings you to the next rock rib and the station for the remaining rappels. Unroped slips here are the danger; keep the party close and move one at a time where it steepens.
Two more rappels put you onto the East Ledges proper. Some parties make a sixth rappel in place of a little downclimbing; either works on a single rope.

Traverse east along sandy, grassy and loose ledges well below the ridge crest, crossing about five rock ribs with short 4th-class moves at each. After the first two ribs there are usually a higher and a lower set of cairns marking the easiest crossing. Stay near one level: too low runs into cliffs above the Boston Glacier, too high into steeper, more corrugated ribs and gullies. The ground is largely unprotectable.

pitch_detail.pitch: Gully to the East Ridge crest
pitch_detail.notes: At the end of the ledges a short gully climbs back up to the East Ridge crest at the saddle beside the solitary gendarme. Following the higher line of cairns lets a party skip the 4th-class red gully at the end and scramble up blocks to the crest instead.

From the crest, descend the East Ridge's standard approach line into Boston Basin: high-friction granite slabs strewn with loose grit and pebbles, then a loose gully. Move from one sheltered spot to the next so no one is below a partner when rocks are knocked down.

review.changed: Kept the four stored labels and corrected the 'Ledges' direction (the ledges are followed EAST toward the gendarme, not westward). Added the gully back to the ridge crest and the final descent into Boston Basin, which the stored table stopped short of. 4 → 6 entries.
review.other_findings: The stored 'Ledges' note said 'working westward', which contradicts the route's own beta and descent_text (ledges followed east to the East Ridge). Stored length_m 260 is unexplained by any source. This row is a descent line, not an ascent — worth confirming it should be a separate climbable route at all.

pitch_detail.notes: Cross the Cascade River on the log a short way downstream of the parking area (slick when wet, exposed in high water), then follow the climbers' path straight up through heavy timber, gaining about 1,500 ft before it breaks out onto talus near 4,000 ft.

Climb north up the boulder field on cairns, staying climber's right to avoid crossing Eldorado Creek; it can hold snow into early summer. The talus eases into Eldorado Creek Basin (camps 5,400–5,600 ft). Cross the ridge above at about 6,100–6,200 ft into Roush Basin, then take talus and slabs to the toe of the Eldorado Glacier; the highest camps sit near the East Ridge at about 7,800 ft.

Rope up where the route reaches the Eldorado Glacier near 6,800 ft. Climb it to about 7,500 ft, where it flattens into the Inspiration Glacier, then cross the Inspiration's southern edge toward the low gap near the east end of Eldorado's East Ridge. Snow bridges soften fast as the day warms, and in late season the glaciers melt out into heavy crevassing that forces much zigzagging.

pitch_detail.pitch: Through the gap to the summit ridge
pitch_detail.notes: Pass north through the gap, then climb west for roughly the last 1,000 vertical ft on the glacier slopes north of the ridge, keeping the crest on your left. Switchback and probe suspect snow bridges. Late in the season this slope can be too broken to pass, and parties scramble a few hundred feet up the rock ridge to regain the snow. It steepens just below the knife-edge; pickets are useful.

The final crest narrows to the famous snow knife-edge, in some conditions very thin and corniced, with steep drops on both sides to the small summit (8,868 ft). Axe and crampons are essential; many parties belay or place pickets along it. Late in the season it can be icy and firm, which makes the same crest more serious to reverse on the way down.

review.changed: Kept the four stored labels (including the two approach stages the table already carried) and filled each with elevations, route-finding and hazards. Split the old single final row: the glacier climb from the gap to the base of the arête is now its own stage. 4 → 5 entries.
review.other_findings: Stored grade 'Class 3' understates the finish slightly — sources treat the arête as steep exposed snow needing axe, crampons and often pickets, not a class 3 scramble. Stored length_m 305 matches roughly the final ~1,000 ft above the gap, not the route from high camp.

pitch_detail.notes: From the bivy col, drop about 200 ft to talus and cross the thin, crevassed glacier remnant below the ridge's gendarmes (exposed to icefall; roughly an hour on snow). A steep gully with class 4 moves at its base and class 3 above reaches the notch at about 6,080 ft where roped climbing starts; the red ledges left of the obvious gully are the better line up it.

An easy ramp off the notch: traverse right along a ledge, then climb up downward-sloping blocks with little protection. A variation to the left, through a small tree, has better holds and is the more secure choice for a less confident leader.
Straight up on big jugs and good footholds to a bush at the top, with solid rock and plenty of placements. The pitch finishes near a small bivy ledge on the ridge.
An easy 4th-class gully on the left with some 5th-class moves above, then easier ground and snow fins along the crest. Most parties simul-climb this stretch; keep gear in on the exposed sections.
The second steep rise on the ridge: solid rock with pockets and ledges where you need them. Small towers follow, with the knife-edge crest ahead.

The poorly protected pitch (often called PG13): traverse down and right around the first gendarme on an exposed ramp on the right side of the ridge, over mossy, lichen-covered and sometimes wet slabs and turf. Protection is marginal and rope drag builds quickly; extend placements.
Climb the second tower on solid rock with big exposure. The top offers a crack for a gear belay, which is more trustworthy than slinging a loose horn.
Steep, clean climbing on solid rock with small holds and good feet, well protected. It ends at the base of the offwidth crux.

A vertical offwidth crack with a large chockstone that feels closer to canyoneering than ridge climbing; it protects well with cams to #2–#3 and many take climbing shoes for it. The bypass traverse right around a horn crosses 15–20 ft of unprotectable slab and is not the easier option. Finish on steep smears onto slab.

Above the offwidth a slab wall with finger cracks can be climbed directly, but moving right and scrambling is faster. A thin, sharp ledge then leads to the great notch, traversing above the West Face with huge exposure on loose rock.

From the great notch, make a short 4th-class step on the right to a faint path, then go diagonally left up class 3–4 ledges and heather toward the south ridge and the small summit. The difficulty is low but the heather-covered rock is loose and a fall would be serious; many parties keep the rope on.

review.changed: Same 11 labels; every note rewritten with features, protection and hazards. Removed all stored lengthM values: the nine pitches were a uniform 30 m each and the two stages 145 m / 73 m, none of which any source gives. Non-token grade strings ('5th (easy)', '4th-5th', '5.6 PG13', 'Low 5th/3rd-4th') replaced with single tokens, PG13 moved to notes.
review.other_findings: The pitch split P1–P9 follows one party's rope-lengths; other parties simul-climb the whole lower ridge in one or two blocks, so the pitch count is a guide, not a fixed topo. The route page grades the route 5.6 PG13; the stored grade already notes '(sometimes rated 5.6)'. The stored 30 m lengths feed the planner estimate and were unsourced — the planner should fall back to its default for this route.

wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge.skip_reason: No pitch-level description exists online: the only route page (Mountain Project 119579098) gives 1,600 ft / 6 pitches / 5.8- and says only 'see Beckey's guide', with no comments; two photo captions say the last pitch is 5.8 PG13 and that the party went right of the line. No trip report of this ridge was found — every McMillan trip report is the West Ridge scramble. Other finding: the stored per-pitch lengths (60/70/90/90/90/85 m) sum to exactly the page's 485 m total and look like an invented split; pitches of 85–90 m are also not single rope-lengths. They feed the planner and should be reviewed/removed by a human. The crux grade cell '5.8- PG13 (crux)' is not a grade token.

pitch_detail.notes: The ice step hides in a cleft on the right side of a buttress, just up and right of the Cosley-Houston. It starts as rambling WI3, then makes a steeper rightward traverse at WI4 to WI4+ before easing into stemming to the lip. The first ascent split it into three pitches on hanging screw belays; in good ice it has gone as one full 70 m rope-length. Bring plenty of screws.

Above the lip, follow optional ice in the gully, then trend up and left onto steep snow gullies with good steps but little protection; pickets are the useful gear here and for anchors. Cross a narrow knife-edge rib and traverse left to join the Cosley-Houston exit. In sun, ice and snow come off the face above in large chunks.
Finish up the last stretch of the Cosley-Houston couloir to the summit on steep snow, commonly simul-climbed with pickets for protection. Do not plan to reverse the ice step.

Collapsed the ice to one '1-3' entry carrying the sourced 70 m length and the described WI3 → WI4/4+ → easing progression, kept the snow gullies and the ~100 ft Cosley-Houston finish as stages. 4 → 3 entries; the dropped rows were the same ice described as three segments with invented numbers.

Descent is not documented by any source for this route specifically — the 'Cosley-Houston finish' note only points back to that route's own descent, which a human should confirm is stored on the Cosley-Houston row.
